---
title: "Set 18 — dashboards, uncertainty, and the story"
subtitle: "After lecture 21 · 11 December · about 40 minutes"
---

No dataset. Bring your churn results from Sets 14 to 17.

## 1 · One figure, three audiences

Take your single best figure and produce three versions: for the data team, for
the marketing director, for the board.

What changed between them? If the answer is only the font size, you have not
done the exercise — say what you *removed* each time and why.

## 2 · Put the uncertainty in

Your model reports a churn probability per customer. Add an interval, or a
calibration plot, or a decile table with observed rates — whichever is honest
for your model.

Then answer: what does a manager do differently on seeing that a prediction of
0.7 is really "somewhere between 0.5 and 0.85"?

## 3 · The number that changes a decision

A dashboard with twelve tiles is a dashboard nobody reads.

Choose the **one** number that should be largest on the page, and defend it
against two rivals you rejected. Tie your choice to an action somebody takes on
a Monday.

## 4 · The sentence under the chart

Write the caption for your main figure: one sentence, stating what the reader
should conclude, not what the chart contains.

"Churn by tenure" is a label. "Customers leave in the first six months, and
almost nowhere else" is a caption. Write captions.

## 5 · Defend it

In pairs: present your figure in ninety seconds. Your partner asks the two
hardest questions they can, one of which must be *"how do you know?"*

Write down the question you could not answer well. That is your revision list.

---

*This set checks: that a chart is an argument, that uncertainty shown is
uncertainty managed, and that the caption is the part people remember.*
